newsitem.title: USA: Wells Fargo warns on second-quarter earnings.
newsitem.headline: Wells Fargo warns on second-quarter earnings.

text.p: Banking giant Wells Fargo & Co. Wednesday said its second-quarter profits will be about 30 percent below first-quarter levels due to unexpected expenses related to its $11 billion acquisition of First Interstate last year.
The news, issued before the stock market opened, confirmed what many on Wall Street had already suspected -- that the merger between Wells Fargo and First Interstate has been far from smooth.
Shares of San Francisco-based Wells Fargo tumbled $14.50 to $264.50 on fears the bank's problems may extend beyond the second quarter.

"We have been in the camp that there's not a quick fix at the bank," said analyst Thomas Theurkauf, with Keefe, Bruyette & Woods Inc. in New York. "I hope I'm wrong but I think that when you run into problems of this sort your competitors can feed off of that literaly for months and months, so I don't think they're out of the woods yet."

In a brief statement, Wells said second-quarter earnings will be about $1 a share below industry analysts' consensus of $3.53 per share. In the second quarter of 1996, Wells earned $363 million, or $3.61 a share.

Wells, the nation's eight-largest bank, attributed the second-quarter shortfall to one-time, unexpected expenses resulting from the resolution of "various operational and back-office issues related to the First Interstate integration, including clearing accounts with other banks."
Wells Fargo has faced continued problems integrating First Interstate since it acquired it in a hostile takeover deal in April 1996.
Analysts said in order to top the friendly offer made by First Bank System Inc. for First Interstate, Wells needed to sweeten its bid, and then look for deep cost cuts.

"To make the numbers work, they had to cut deep and fast into the cost structure of First Interstate," Theurkauf said. "When you do that, you bear executional risk, and they're paying the price for that executional risk."
Indeed, over the last few months, many customers have defected to rival banks because of service issues.
News of the second-quarter problems is the latest in a series of bad news to hit Wells Fargo recently.

In May, billionaire investor Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway Inc. sold 265,000 shares of Wells Fargo, reducing his stake in the bank to around 7.8 percent. Word of the sale was followed the next day by news that President William Zuendt, one of the architects of the First Interstate acquisition, planned to retire later this year.
